description:
Found while fixing fz-5xp.33.

Every BINARY arithmetic operator is a typed clause family in kernel.fz:

    fn left :: integer - right :: integer, do: fz_op_sub_ii(left, right)
    fn left :: float   - right :: float,   do: fz_op_sub_ff(left, right)
    ... (fz-5xp.18)

Runtime clause dispatch then picks the right one, so a dynamically-typed
operand works. UNARY minus has no family. It is lowered straight to
`Prim::UnOp(Neg)` in native codegen, which reads ONE lane.

Measured, one call site each, same program shape:

    fnp pick(0), do: 4.5
    fnp pick(_), do: 9

    dbg(0 - pick(0))     interp -4.5   run -4.5   build -4.5
    dbg(-pick(0))        interp -4.5   run ABORT  build ABORT

Subtracting from zero works and negating does not, which is the definition of
one question with two implementations. fz-5xp.33 gave `Prim::UnOp(Neg)` a float
lane, so every case where the operand's lane is known statically now agrees on
all three doors; a union operand still aborts natively.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE GOAL PROGRAM: a JSON number parser negates a value that
may be integer or float depending on the text it just scanned. That is exactly
the union shape above.

DO IT THE WAY THE BINARY OPERATORS WERE DONE. The user's rule when fz-5xp.18
settled this for comparisons: "if we remove the special-casing for <, <=, etc.
and treat them as function calls, then unsupported combinations will be compiler
errors." The same applies here, and it retires `Prim::UnOp(Neg)`'s hand-written
lanes rather than adding a third.

SHAPE. Needs `fz_op_neg_i` / `fz_op_neg_f` externs plus their shims and
`RUNTIME_SYMBOLS` rows, and a decision about the surface: kernel.fz's operator
clauses are all INFIX (`fn left :: integer + right :: integer`), so either the
parser learns prefix operator clauses, or the front door rewrites `-x` to a
named call the way `source_sugar.rs` already rewrites `<>`, `++`, `in` and
friends. The second is smaller and uses machinery that exists.

WATCH OUT: `-0.0` must stay `-0.0`. That rules out the tempting rewrite of `-x`
to `0 - x`, which turns it into `0.0`. Check `UnOp::Not` at the same time -- it
is the other unary and was never examined.
title: Unary minus is the last operator not routed through Kernel
